Linear Dependencies in Weyl-Heisenberg Orbits

Hoan Bui Dang Affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics, Waterloo, Ontario N2L 2Y5, Canada    Kate Blanchfield    Ingemar Bengtsson    D. M. Appleby Affiliation: Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics, Waterloo, Ontario N2L 2Y5, Canada Affiliation: Physics Department, University of Waterloo, Ontario N2L 3G1, Canada Affiliation: Stockholms universitet, AlbaNova, Fysikum, S-106 91 Stockholm, Sweden
Abstract

Five years ago, Lane Hughston showed that some of the symmetric informationally complete positive operator valued measures (SICs) in dimension 3 coincide with the Hesse configuration (a structure well known to algebraic geometers, which arises from the torsion points of a certain elliptic curve). This connection with elliptic curves is signalled by the presence of linear dependencies among the SIC vectors. Here we look for analogous connections between SICs and algebraic geometry by performing computer searches for linear dependencies in higher dimensional SICs. We prove that linear dependencies will always emerge in Weyl-Heisenberg orbits when the fiducial vector lies in a certain subspace of an order 3 unitary matrix. This includes SICs when the dimension is divisible by 3 or equal to 8 mod 9. We examine the linear dependencies in dimension 6 in detail and show that smaller dimensional SICs are contained within this structure, potentially impacting the SIC existence problem. We extend our results to look for linear dependencies in orbits when the fiducial vector lies in an eigenspace of other elements of the Clifford group that are not order 3. Finally, we align our work with recent studies on representations of the Clifford group.

1 Introduction

Symmetric informationally-complete positive operator-valued measures (SICs) [1, 2] represent a general form of measurement in quantum theory. As the more familiar projective measurements are associated to an orthonormal basis in Hilbert space, a SIC is associated to an over-complete set of N2N^{2} unit vectors in ℋN\mathcal{H}^{N} such that the absolute value of the scalar product between any distinct two is always constant, i.e.

∑ν=0N2−11N​|ψν⟩​⟨ψν|=𝟙\sum_{\nu=0}^{N^{2}-1}\frac{1}{N}|\psi_{\nu}\rangle\langle\psi_{\nu}|={\mathbbm{1}} (1)
|⟨ψν|ψμ⟩|={1ifν=μ1N+1ifν≠μ\left|\left\langle\psi_{\nu}|\psi_{\mu}\right\rangle\right|=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&\mbox{if}&\mbox{{\small$\nu=\mu$}}\\ \ \frac{1}{\sqrt{N+1}}&\mbox{if}&\mbox{{\small$\nu\neq\mu$}}\end{array}\right. (2)

SICs have practical applications in quantum state tomography [3, 4], quantum communication [5, 6], quantum cryptography [7, 8], classical high precision radar [9, 10] and classical speech recognition [11]. A significant amount of work is aimed towards proving their existence in all dimensions although no general proof is currently known. Numerical studies have successfully found SICs when N≤67N\leq 67 [12] and analytical solutions have been published for 20 of these dimensions (see references in [12] plus recent solutions for N=16N=16 in [13] and N=28N=28 in [14]). Such results promote the belief that SICs can always be found, but the current solutions are rather dimension-dependent and do not provide an overall coherent picture.

All known SICs are group covariant, meaning they can be obtained from the action of a group on a single fiducial vector. The vast majority of SICs are covariant with respect to the Weyl-Heisenberg (WH) group and if the dimension is a prime, it has been shown this is the only possible group [15]. In this paper we only consider such SICs.

There are a few curious properties of SICs that are not yet understood, but clearly hint at an underlying mathematical structure. This scenario could support suggestions that SICs should play a deeper role in quantum mechanics [16]. The most well-known of these properties is the conjecture of Zauner symmetry, which states that every SIC vector is an eigenvector of a certain order three unitary matrix [12, 17, 1]. Another property stems from current SIC solutions; in a preferred basis, the components of the SIC vectors are expressed as nested radicals. Such complex numbers are quite exceptional and arise because the Galois group of the polynomial equation one must solve is solvable [12, 18]. However, it is a third observation that we shall focus on in this paper, namely the connection between SICs and algebraic curves in dimension 3.

The WH group appears naturally in the theory of elliptic curves [19], suggesting this might be an advantageous framework for the study of SICs. Furthermore, there is a very close connection between elliptic curves and linear dependencies among SIC vectors in dimension 3, first noted by Lane Hughston [20]. This leads to the Hesse configuration in the complex projective plane—a particular structure well-known in algebraic geometry. We aim to explore this special connection, looking for analogous linear dependencies in higher dimensions. It was our hope that another configuration in complex projective space might reveal some new structure behind SICs and broaden the areas from which they can be studied. This did not turn out quite as planned for all the SICs we looked at but we do see similarities for certain SICs in dimension 8, which could signal another connection to elliptic curves. No sets of NN linearly dependent SIC vectors exist for N=4N=4, 5 or 7, but we do find them again when N=6N=6, 9 and 12—however, in these latter cases the linear dependencies are not uniquely tied to SICs. Additionally, we found an unexpected method of generating 2- and 3-dimensional SICs from the linear dependencies among vectors in 6- and 9-dimensional SICs, respectively. We don’t know whether this can be generalised to all dimensions divisible by 3.

We observe that the reverse of our problem—to show that there exists an open set of fiducials giving rise to WH orbits without linear dependencies—has been considered for signal processing purposes and has been solved in prime dimensions [21, 22] and more recently in all finite dimension [23].

In section 2 we review some basic facts about the Weyl-Heisenberg and Clifford groups, and explain notations and terminology used in the rest of the paper. Section 3 introduces the Hesse configuration and linear dependencies in SICs in dimension 3. Section 4 proves that linear dependencies can always be found in WH orbits when the fiducial vector is an eigenvector of an order 3 unitary matrix. In dimensions divisible by 3 and dimensions equal to 8 mod 9, these WH orbits include SICs. In section 5, we give numerical results from our computer search for dependencies in dimensions 4 to 9. We focus specifically on data relating to the SIC case in dimensions 6 and 9. In section 6, we prove the sets of linearly dependent vectors in dimension 6 contain 2-dimensional SICs and show that sets in dimension 9 contain 3-dimensional SICs. We do not have data for dimension 12 or higher, so do not know whether this pattern continues for all dimensions divisible by 3. In which case, this could open a new avenue for a SIC existence proof. Section 7 turns away from SICs altogether and proves that linear dependencies will always arise in WH orbits with a fiducial vector invariant under a unitary matrix whose order is a non-trivial divisor of NN in dimensions where NN is a product of distinct prime numbers. We give an example of this using linear dependencies in even dimensions. Section 8 relates our results to a recent representation of the Clifford group [13]. Section 9 summarises our results and points at some possible clues for the SIC existence problem.

As mentioned in the Introduction it turns out that every known WH SIC fiducial vector is an eigenvector of a canonical order 33 Clifford unitary and, conversely, that in every dimension where an exhaustive search has been made every canonical order 33 Clifford unitary has a SIC fiducial vector as one of its eigenvectors [17, 12]. 3 Linear dependencies in dimension 3

Lane Hughston showed that vectors in some 3-dimensional SICs coincide exactly with the nine inflection points of a particular family of elliptic curves [20]. The pattern of linear dependencies among the SIC vectors reproduces the Hesse configuration [25, 26] and so we shall first look in more detail at linear dependencies coming from SICs in dimension 3. This section forms our motivation for studying higher dimensional dependency structures and, although SICs in dimension 3 have been studied fairly extensively before now [15, 17], we hope the following approach provides a useful way of looking at things.

In dimension 3, there is a continuous one-parameter family of SICs. The nine explicit (un-normalised) vectors are the columns of the matrix

[000−ei​θ−ei​θ​η−ei​θ​η2111111000−ei​θ−ei​θ​η−ei​θ​η2−ei​θ−ei​θ​η−ei​θ​η2111000]\left[\begin{array}[]{ccccccccc}0&0&0&-e^{i\theta}&-e^{i\theta}\eta&-e^{i\theta}\eta^{2}&1&1&1\\ 1&1&1&0&0&0&-e^{i\theta}&-e^{i\theta}\eta&-e^{i\theta}\eta^{2}\\ -e^{i\theta}&-e^{i\theta}\eta&-e^{i\theta}\eta^{2}&1&1&1&0&0&0\\ \end{array}\right] (22)

The parameter θ\theta needs only be considered in the interval [0,2​π6][0,\frac{2\pi}{6}] as all other SICs are equivalent to these via transformations in the extended Clifford group. It is clear from inspection that any such SIC in dimension 3 will have three sets of three linearly dependent vectors. However, there are additional dependencies for certain choices of θ\theta. We can find these values by setting the determinant of any three other SIC vectors to zero. This gives

|0−ei​θ​ηm110−ei​θ​ηn−ei​θ​ηk10|=1−e3​i​θ​ηk+m+n=0\left|\begin{array}[]{ccc}0&-e^{i\theta}\eta^{m}&1\\ 1&0&-e^{i\theta}\eta^{n}\\ -e^{i\theta}\eta^{k}&1&0\\ \end{array}\right|=1-e^{3i\theta}\eta^{k+m+n}=0 (23)

and we find the condition

e3​i​θ=ηrr∈{0,1,2}e^{3i\theta}=\eta^{r}\quad\quad r\in\left\{0,1,2\right\} (24)

Given our limits for θ\theta, we are left with the options θ=0\theta=0 or 2​π9\frac{2\pi}{9} in order to obtain a ‘special’ SIC with 12 sets of three linearly dependent vectors. The SIC with θ=0\theta=0 is a particularly special case as its fiducial vector

|ϕ⟩=(01−1)|\phi\rangle=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ 1\\ -1\\ \end{array}\right) (25)

is invariant under all symplectic unitaries. We can see this by rewriting the projector onto this vector as

|ϕ⟩​⟨ϕ|=𝟙−U𝒫𝒫=(−100−1)|\phi\rangle\langle\phi|=\mathbbm{1}-U_{\mathcal{P}}\quad\quad\mathcal{P}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}-1&0\\ 0&-1\\ \end{array}\right) (26)

The matrix 𝒫\mathcal{P} is called the parity matrix, and its unitary representative U𝒫U_{\mathcal{P}} is one of the phase-point operators introduced by Wootters [27]. It is unique in being the only element (other than the identity element) invariant under conjugation by every other element in the symplectic group and so, with the identity element, forms the group’s centre. As the right hand side of the first of Equations (26) is invariant under S​L​(2,ℤN)SL(2,{\mathbbm{Z}}_{N}), the SIC fiducial vector |ϕ⟩|\phi\rangle must be an eigenvector of every symplectic unitary matrix. Of interest to us is its invariance under the action of the symplectic canonical order 3 unitaries. There are eight such unitaries altogether (including the Zauner unitary) but we consider the four unitaries

U(1011)=(η00010001),U(0212)=ei​π63​(111η21ηη2η1)\displaystyle U_{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\ 1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}\eta&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\end{array}\right)\quad U_{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&2\\ 1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)}=\frac{e^{\frac{i\pi}{6}}}{\sqrt{3}}\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&1&1\\ \eta^{2}&1&\eta\\ \eta^{2}&\eta&1\end{array}\right)
(34)
U(2210)=ei​π63​(1η2η211η1η1)U(1201)=ei​π63​(1ηηη1ηηη1)\displaystyle U_{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&2\\ 1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)}=\frac{e^{\frac{i\pi}{6}}}{\sqrt{3}}\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&\eta^{2}&\eta^{2}\\ 1&1&\eta\\ 1&\eta&1\end{array}\right)\quad U_{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\ 0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)}=\frac{e^{\frac{i\pi}{6}}}{\sqrt{3}}\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1&\eta&\eta\\ \eta&1&\eta\\ \eta&\eta&1\end{array}\right)

since the other four are squares of these. Note that U(0212)U_{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&2\\ 1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)} corresponds to the Zauner matrix in Equation (19) of Section 2. The SIC fiducial defined in Equation (25) is then precisely the intersection point of the 2-dimensional subspaces ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} from each of these four symplectic canonical order 3 unitaries. We can then ask whether any other SIC vectors are also contained within these same subspaces. It turns out that the remaining SIC vectors are distributed evenly amongst the subspaces: 2 further vectors per unitary subspace.

When we view the full SIC as a 3×33\times 3 lattice in the complex projective plane (where each point is a SIC vector and each line is a 2-dimensional subspace) we generate the Hesse configuration. In Figure 1, the fiducial vector is found at the point at the bottom left of the plane. The left-hand image shows the three linear dependencies in every dimension 3 SIC while the right-hand image shows the pattern of symplectic canonical order 3 unitary subspaces that intersect at the fiducial vector |ϕ⟩|\phi\rangle, i.e. the SIC fiducial for which θ=0\theta=0. The Clifford group also contains WH conjugates of the form Dp​U​Dp†D_{p}UD_{p}^{\dagger}, where UU is one of the four unitaries in Equation (27), and in this way we find a total of 12 order three unitaries and hence 12 subspaces. Remarkably, they always intersect in sets of four at a point described precisely by one of the SIC vectors. We recover the famous Hesse configuration of 9 points and 12 lines in the projective plane [25]. To obtain this full picture from Figure 1, we must translate the lines in the right-hand image. Each line can be translated three times, so we find 12 lines in total.

Hesse originally discovered his configuration by examining elliptic curves. In particular, the family of cubics

x3+y3+z3+λ​x​y​z=0λ∈ℂx^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}+\lambda xyz=0\quad\quad\lambda\in\mathbbm{C} (42)

is invariant under the WH group. It is often called the Hesse pencil of cubics. The points on the curve where the determinant of the Hessian (the matrix containing the second derivatives of the curve) vanish are called inflection points. The determinant of the Hessian is also a cubic in the same family and Bézout’s theorem states that two cubics in ℂ​P2\mathbbm{C}\mathrm{P}^{2} will intersect in nine points. These are the nine inflection points and they coincide exactly with the nine SIC vectors, i.e. then the values of xx, yy and zz in Equation (28) are the components in a SIC vector. The same inflection points (and thus the same SIC) arise for all values of λ\lambda, except for the special cases when λ=∞\lambda=\infty and λ3=−1\lambda^{3}=-1. These special cases give rise to singular members of this family. Each singular curve, TiT_{i}, degenerates into three projective lines

T0:x​y​z=0T1:(x+y+z)​(x+η​y+η2​z)​(x+η2​y+η​z)=0T2:(x+η​y+z)​(x+η2​y+η2​z)​(x+y+η​z)=0T3:(x+η2​y+z)​(x+η​y+η​z)​(x+y+η2​z)=0\begin{array}[]{l}T_{0}:xyz=0\\ T_{1}:(x+y+z)(x+\eta y+\eta^{2}z)(x+\eta^{2}y+\eta z)=0\\ T_{2}:(x+\eta y+z)(x+\eta^{2}y+\eta^{2}z)(x+y+\eta z)=0\\ T_{3}:(x+\eta^{2}y+z)(x+\eta y+\eta z)(x+y+\eta^{2}z)=0\\ \end{array} (43)

Each line passes through three inflection points and each inflection point lies on four lines, forming our familiar Hesse configuration. It is often denoted (94,123)\left(9_{4},12_{3}\right) to reflect the property that the 9 points each lie in 4 lines and the 12 lines each contain 3 points. A more detailed survey of the Hesse configuration is given in [26] and its connection to SICs in [28].

This pattern of subspace intersections has a connection to mutually unbiased bases. Each of the twelve lines in the Hesse configuration represents a 2-dimensional subspace in ℂ3\mathbbm{C}^{3} with an orthogonal vector that is uniquely determined up to a scalar. We shall call this a normal vector from here onwards. These 12 normal vectors reproduce the standard MUB in dimension 3, obtained from the eigenvectors of the cyclic subgroups of the WH group. Note that we use the acronym MUB to mean a complete set of N+1N+1 mutually unbiased bases. As the MUB vectors lie orthogonally to the 2-dimensional eigenspaces, they must sit in the 1-dimensional eigenspace ℋη\mathcal{H}_{\eta}.

So far we have been looking at the single SIC with θ=0\theta=0. However, one also gets a Hesse configuration when θ=2​π9\theta=\frac{2\pi}{9}. Most SICs in dimension 3 are part of an extended Clifford group orbit containing eight SICs [17]. The exceptions are the SICs with θ=0\theta=0 and θ=2​π6\theta=\frac{2\pi}{6} in Equation (22), which lie on orbits containing one and four SICs, respectively. The ‘special SIC’, with θ=2​π9\theta=\frac{2\pi}{9}, is then on an extended Clifford orbit with seven other SICs and all eight of these SICs are special in the sense that they have 12 linearly dependent sets of three vectors. This extends to the MUB connection. Above, we found a MUB from the normal vectors—lines in the Hesse configuration—of linear dependencies in the ‘special SIC’ with θ=0\theta=0. Note that this MUB is itself a single orbit of the extended Clifford group. We can extract eight more MUBs in the same way from the other eight ‘special SICs’. They can be arrived at in a different way. The Clifford group contains altogether 36 order 3 subgroups with elements of the form D𝐩​UD_{\bf p}U, with UU a symplectic order 3 unitary. So far we have used only 12 of these. The remaining 24 have non-degenerate spectra, and their eigenbases can be collected into 8 sets of 3 mutually unbiased bases. Each such triplet is in itself an orbit under the WH group, and forms a MUB when a basis from the standard MUB is added [29, 30]. This ties in exactly with the eight ‘special SICs’ with θ=2​π9\theta=\frac{2\pi}{9} through the Hesse configuration [30]. Each SIC, together with one of these WH orbit MUBs, reproduces the pattern (94,123)\left(9_{4},12_{3}\right). It is perhaps interesting to note that we could have arrived at the nine ‘special SICs’ from knowledge of the symplectic canonical order 3 unitaries and the additional WH orbit MUBs alone.

4 Linear dependencies from the eigenvectors of U𝒵U_{\mathcal{Z}}

In this section we show how linear dependencies will arise in every dimension. The results in this section apply to all orbits in which the fiducial vector lies in certain eigenspaces of U𝒵U_{\mathcal{Z}}, depending on the dimension, and not only to SIC fiducials.

From Section 2, we can label a vector in a WH orbit, up to a phase, by a 2-component vector 𝐩{\bf p} in ℤN2\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{2}. In this representation, we are interested in the orbit of 𝐩{\bf p} under the action of 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. If 𝐩{\bf p} is one of the fixed points of 𝒵\mathcal{Z} it will form a singlet, otherwise {𝐩,𝒵​𝐩,𝒵2​𝐩}\{{\bf p},\mathcal{Z}{\bf p},\mathcal{Z}^{2}{\bf p}\} forms a triplet since 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is of order 3. If the dimension NN is divisible by 3, 𝒵\mathcal{Z} has exactly 3 singlets, which are given by Equation (21). In other dimensions, the only singlet is 𝐩=(0,0){\bf p}=(0,0). In the Hilbert space, we will use the same terminology to call D𝐩|ψ⟩D_{\bf{p}}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle a singlet if 𝐩{\bf p} is a singlet, and to call {D𝐩|ψ⟩,D𝒵​𝐩|ψ⟩,D𝒵2​𝐩|ψ⟩}\{D_{\bf p}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle,D_{\mathcal{Z}{\bf p}}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle,D_{\mathcal{Z}^{2}{\bf p}}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle\} a triplet otherwise.

Theorem 1.

In dimension N=3​kN=3k any subset of NN vectors in a WH orbit whose fiducial vector is an eigenvector of U𝒵U_{\mathcal{Z}} is linearly dependent if it contains kk triplets, or k−1k-1 triplets and 3 singlets.

Proof.

Let N=3​kN=3k and let U𝒵|ψ0⟩=λ|ψ0⟩U_{\mathcal{Z}}\left|{\psi_{0}}\right\rangle=\lambda\left|{\psi_{0}}\right\rangle. When 𝐩{\bf p} is a singlet, D𝐩|ψ0⟩D_{\bf p}\left|{\psi_{0}}\right\rangle lies in the same eigenspace of U𝒵U_{\mathcal{Z}} as |ψ0⟩\left|{\psi_{0}}\right\rangle because

U𝒵D𝐩|ψ0⟩=U𝒵D𝐩U𝒵†U𝒵|ψ0⟩=λD𝒵​𝐩|ψ0⟩=λD𝐩|ψ0⟩U_{\mathcal{Z}}D_{\bf p}\left|{\psi_{0}}\right\rangle=U_{\mathcal{Z}}D_{\bf p}U_{\mathcal{Z}}^{\dagger}U_{\mathcal{Z}}\left|{\psi_{0}}\right\rangle=\lambda D_{\mathcal{Z}{\bf p}}\left|{\psi_{0}}\right\rangle=\lambda D_{\bf p}\left|{\psi_{0}}\right\rangle (44)

When 𝐩{\bf p} is in a triplet, we construct three new linear combinations of vectors in the triplet {D𝐩|ψ⟩,D𝒵​𝐩|ψ⟩,D𝒵2​𝐩|ψ⟩}\{D_{\bf p}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle,D_{\mathcal{Z}{\bf p}}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle,D_{\mathcal{Z}^{2}{\bf p}}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle\}. Our vectors are

|r⟩=D𝐩|ψ0⟩+U𝒵D𝐩|ψ0⟩+U𝒵2D𝐩|ψ0⟩\left|r\right\rangle=D_{\bf{p}}\left|\psi_{0}\right\rangle+U_{\mathcal{Z}}D_{\bf{p}}\left|\psi_{0}\right\rangle+U_{\mathcal{Z}}^{2}D_{\bf{p}}\left|\psi_{0}\right\rangle
|s⟩=D𝐩|ψ0⟩+η2U𝒵D𝐩|ψ0⟩+ηU𝒵2D𝐩|ψ0⟩\left|s\right\rangle=D_{\bf{p}}\left|\psi_{0}\right\rangle+\eta^{2}U_{\mathcal{Z}}D_{\bf{p}}\left|\psi_{0}\right\rangle+\eta U_{\mathcal{Z}}^{2}D_{\bf{p}}\left|\psi_{0}\right\rangle (45)
|t⟩=D𝐩|ψ0⟩+ηU𝒵D𝐩|ψ0⟩+η2U𝒵2D𝐩|ψ0⟩\left|t\right\rangle=D_{\bf{p}}\left|\psi_{0}\right\rangle+\eta U_{\mathcal{Z}}D_{\bf{p}}\left|\psi_{0}\right\rangle+\eta^{2}U_{\mathcal{Z}}^{2}D_{\bf{p}}\left|\psi_{0}\right\rangle

where η=e2​π​i3\eta=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{3}}. We will refer to vectors constructed in this way, for a given choice of p, as rr-type, ss-type and tt-type respectively. It is straightforward to check that these vectors are evenly distributed among the three eigenspaces ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}, ℋη\mathcal{H}_{\eta} and ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}}, shown in Table 1. It is also clear that the linear span of the vectors {D𝐩|ψ0⟩,D𝒵​𝐩|ψ0⟩,D𝒵2​𝐩|ψ0⟩}\{D_{\bf{p}}\left|{\psi_{0}}\right\rangle,D_{\mathcal{Z}\bf{p}}\left|{\psi_{0}}\right\rangle,D_{\mathcal{Z}^{2}\bf{p}}\left|{\psi_{0}}\right\rangle\} equals that of the vectors {|r⟩,|s⟩,|t⟩}\{\left|{r}\right\rangle,\left|{s}\right\rangle,\left|{t}\right\rangle\}.

If a set of NN vectors contains kk triplets, this gives kk-many of each rr-,ss-, and tt-type vector. From Table 1 we know that the rr-type vectors lie in an eigenspace of dimension k+1k+1, the ss-type vectors lie in an eigenspace of dimension kk, and the tt-type vectors lie in an eigenspace of dimension k−1k-1. It is clear then that the kk rr-type vectors cannot fully span their subspace while the kk tt-type vectors are overcomplete and therefore linearly dependent.

If a set contains k−1k-1 triplets and 33 singlets, this gives (k−1)(k-1)-many of each rr-,ss-, and tt-type vector, plus the 3 singlets that are in the same eigenspace as the fiducial vector |ψ0⟩\left|{\psi_{0}}\right\rangle. Therefore there will be k+2k+2 vectors lying in the same eigenspace. Since the largest eigenspace of U𝒵U_{\mathcal{Z}} has dimensionality k+1k+1, this results in linear dependency. ∎

When the fiducial vector lies in ℋη\mathcal{H}_{\eta} or ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}} we can obtain dependencies using fewer than NN vectors. For example, if |ψ0⟩∈ℋη\left|{\psi_{0}}\right\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{\eta} then linear dependency will also occur when the set contains k−1k-1 triplets and 22 singlets, or k−2k-2 triplets and 33 singlets. And if |ψ0⟩∈ℋη2\left|{\psi_{0}}\right\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}}, linear dependency will also occur when the set contains k−1k-1 triplets and 11 singlet, k−2k-2 triplets and 22 singlets, or k−3k-3 triplets and 33 singlets.

If the dimension is not divisible by 3 the matrix 𝒵\mathcal{Z} has only one fixed point. Nevertheless WH orbits with linear dependencies do arise.

Theorem 2.

In dimension N=3​k+1N=3k+1 any subset of NN vectors in a WH orbit whose fiducial vector lies in the eigenspace ℋη\mathcal{H}_{\eta} or ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}} is linearly dependent if it contains kk triplets and 1 singlet.

Proof.

In dimension N=3​k+1N=3k+1, the three eigenspaces ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}, ℋη\mathcal{H}_{\eta} and ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}} have dimensionality k+1k+1, kk, and kk, respectively. If the fiducial lies in ℋη\mathcal{H}_{\eta}, which is the only singlet in this case, then together with kk ss-type vectors it will give k+1k+1 vectors in this subspace, resulting in linear dependency. The same argument applies when the fiducial vector lies in ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}}. ∎

Theorem 3.

In dimension N=3​k+2N=3k+2 any subset of N−1N-1 vectors in a WH orbit whose fiducial vector lies in the eigenspace ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}} is linearly dependent if it contains kk triplets and 1 singlet.

Proof.

In dimension N=3​k+2N=3k+2, the eigenspace ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}} has dimensionality kk. The kk tt-type vectors, together with the fiducial vector, form a set of k+1k+1 vectors in ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}}, thus they are linearly dependent. ∎

Lastly, we note that if a set is linearly dependent, all other sets in its WH orbit are also linearly dependent. In Theorem 1, sets that contain kk triplets, or k−1k-1 triplets and 33 singlets, have the property that they remain invariant (as sets) under the action of U𝒵U_{\mathcal{Z}}. We shall refer to these sets as Zauner invariant sets, and their orbits as Zauner invariant orbits.

5 Numerical linear dependencies

In the previous section we proved that we can find NN linearly dependent vectors in a WH orbit when the fiducial vector is in a certain Zauner subspace. However, this doesn’t quite capture the whole picture. In this section, we provide the outcome of our numerical search for linear dependencies in dimensions 4 to 8 (with partial results when N=9N=9 and 12) and give additional linear dependencies that are not covered in the previous section. We are especially interested in dimensions divisible by 3, where dependencies are always found if the fiducial lies in the subspace where we expect the SIC fiducials to be, and we discuss details of linear dependencies in dimensions 6 and 9. The additional dependencies in these dimensions do not depend on whether the WH orbit is a SIC or not, although we find some interesting orthogonality relationships in the dependency structure that are unique to SICs (and hence do not occur in WH orbits starting with a non-SIC fiducial vector in ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}). Our investigation into dependencies in dimensions 6 and 9 also led to smaller-dimensional SICs, but we will postpone a discussion of these until the next section. In dimension 8, there are SIC fiducials in the Zauner subspace ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}} and our numerical data show that these SICs have more linearly dependent sets of 8 vectors than WH orbits with a vector in ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}}. Recall that this was precisely the situation with the ‘special SICs’ in dimension 3 and so could indicate a dimension 8 analogue of the Hesse configuration.

In each dimension NN, our computer program started with a vector from one of the Zauner subspaces, generated the full orbit under the action of the WH group and then performed an exhaustive search for all sets of NN vectors that are linearly dependent. For each subspace of the Zauner unitary in each dimension, we repeated the procedure with a small number of arbitrarily chosen fiducial vectors to ensure that the results are the same for generic fiducials. In the case of SIC vectors, we used the fiducials given in [12]; where there was a choice of Clifford orbits, we repeated the calculation with fiducials from each orbit.

We found no dependence on the choice of fiducial except in dimension 8 where the SIC gives 24,935,160 linear dependencies, which is slightly higher than the generic result given in Table 2. The results often showed a higher number of linear dependencies than accounted for by Theorems 1-3. Table 2 shows the total number of sets of NN linearly dependent vectors in WH orbits with fiducial vectors in different Zauner subspaces. The number predicted by the proofs in the previous section, or an upper bound on this number, is given in brackets. For dimension 9 we were not able to perform an exhaustive search.

Assuming the Zauner conjecture holds, Theorem 1 shows that SICs in dimensions divisible by 3 contain linearly dependent vectors. As we are primarily interested in SICs, we turn to look in more detail at these dimensions. When N=6N=6 there are 984 sets of six linearly dependent SIC vectors, to a numerical precision of 10−1510^{-15}. All the results reported in this section are numerical and hold to within this precision. This is a higher number of dependencies than we proved must exist in the previous section, which finds only 768 of the 984 sets we generated numerically. Recall that the proof required the N vectors in the WH orbit to be invariant under the Zauner unitary or one of its WH conjugates; the additional 216 sets in dimension 6 are not of this form. Curiously, they are instead invariant under an order 6 unitary matrix UℳU_{\mathcal{M}} whose symplectic representation is

ℳ=(38411)\mathcal{M}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ll}3&8\\ 4&11\end{array}\right) (46)

Each of the 36 SIC vectors lies in 164 different sets of linearly dependent SIC vectors, and clearly each of the 984 linearly dependent sets contains 6 vectors. In the language of complex projective space there are 36 points and 984 hyperplanes, forming the balanced configuration (36164,9846)(36_{164},984_{6}). If this constitutes a known pattern in ℂ​P5\mathbbm{C}\mathrm{P}^{5} we do not recognise it.

The 984 linearly dependent sets can themselves be collected into orbits under the WH group. There are 27 orbits of length 36 and 1 orbit of length 12. The short orbit arises because it contains only linearly dependent sets invariant under the subgroup {1,X2​Z4,X4​Z2}\{1,X^{2}Z^{4},X^{4}Z^{2}\}. This subgroup commutes with the Zauner unitary defined in Equations (13) and (19), which leaves the fiducial SIC vector invariant. Twenty two of these WH orbits contain sets that are invariant under the Zauner matrix (or sets invariant under a WH conjugate D𝐩​U𝒵​D𝐩†D_{{\bf p}}U_{\mathcal{Z}}D_{{\bf p}}^{\dagger} of the Zauner matrix); the other 6 are invariant under the action of UℳU_{\mathcal{M}}.

Inspired by the 3-dimensional case, we look at the 984 vectors normal to the linearly dependent sets and perform an exhaustive search for orthogonalities between them. There is no basis among them—nor a MUB!—but there are nine sets of four mutually orthogonal normal vectors. These normal vectors all belong to the same orbit under the WH group (of length 36). Each set of four mutually orthogonal vectors forms an orbit under the subgroup of the WH group that contains order 2 elements only. In addition, there are over 20,000 orthogonal triples of normal vectors, only 712 of which lie in a single WH orbit.

The resulting structure in dimension 6 is summarised in Table 3, where we have labelled each WH orbit from 1 to 28. The first orbit is the short one and we see that every set of six linearly dependent vectors in this orbit is formed from two orbits under the subgroup {1,X2​Z4,X4​Z2}\{1,X^{2}Z^{4},X^{4}Z^{2}\}. The orbit containing the mutually orthogonal normal vectors is number 11, and orbits 23 to 28 are the ones invariant under UℳU_{\mathcal{M}}—they contain sets of six vectors forming just one orbit under U𝒵U_{\mathcal{Z}}, rather than two.

The six-dimensional case shows some similarities to the three-dimensional one, but the pattern is not as striking. We now ask to what extent the results depend on the fact that we start from 36 vectors forming a SIC. From the previous section, we expect the pattern of at least 768 of the 984 sets of linearly dependent vectors to remain unchanged, i.e. the same p vectors to appear in the same sets. To check this, we repeated our calculations starting from a fiducial vector chosen arbitrarily from the Zauner subspace (i.e. in ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}). This will produce 36 vectors typically not forming a SIC. In the cases we looked at, we found all 984 sets of six linearly dependent vectors had exactly the same pattern as when we started with a SIC.

However, there are some subtle differences between SICs and non-SICs in dimension 6, despite the pattern of dependencies being the same when the fiducial is taken arbitrarily from ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}. The four orthogonal quadruples among the normal vectors are present only in the SIC case. An additional 216 orthogonal triples vanish when we pick an arbitrary fiducial from ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}; the triples all have one normal vector in WH orbit 11, one vector from either WH orbit 12 or 13 and the final vector from one of the orbits 23, 24,…\ldots,28. As every normal vector in orbits 23 to 28 are used, we find 6×36=2166\times 36=216 triples. It is perhaps noteworthy that these latter six ‘SIC-sensitive’ WH orbits are precisely the UℳU_{\mathcal{M}} invariant ones.

In dimension 9, the SIC has 79,767 sets of nine linearly dependent vectors. Of these, 78,795 are predicted by Theorem 1 in Section 4. This large number of dependencies meant that we could not perform as complete computer searches as for the dimension 6 case. For example, we did not compute the scalar products between every pair of normal vectors, although we happen to know they form a basis (this is discussed in more detail in section 8). As with the dimension 6 case, we can collect these 79,767 linearly dependent sets into orbits under the WH group. We find 987 WH orbits: 984 of length 81, 2 of length 27 and 1 of length 9. This gives 975 orbits invariant under the action of the Zauner unitary or one of its WH conjugates, with the remaining 12 invariant under UℳU_{\mathcal{M}} (186 orbits are invariant under both types). In odd dimensions where N=3​kN=3k, ℳ\mathcal{M} takes the form

G=(k+1k2​k2​k+1)G=\left(\begin{array}[]{ll}k+1&k\\ 2k&2k+1\end{array}\right) (47)

When we repeat the calculations using an arbitrary vector from ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}, we again find exactly the same pattern of linearly dependent vectors (in the sense that the dependencies are labelled by the same p vectors). This suggests a distinction between SICs in dimension 3 and SICs in higher dimensions divisible by 3. ‘Special SICs’ in dimension 3 gave rise to 12 sets of linear dependencies, while the others produced only 3. No SICs are ‘special’ in this sense in dimensions 6 and 9; instead we find that not only do all SICs have the same pattern of linearly dependent vectors, but this pattern can be be almost completely reproduced by acting with the WH group on any vector in the Zauner subspace (the pattern of orthogonalities among normal vectors cannot be reproduced). However, we did find one other instance of a SIC fiducial vector giving more linear dependencies than other vectors in the same subspace. In dimension 8, there is a SIC sitting in another eigenspace of the Zauner unitary, namely the one with the smallest dimension, ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}}. This SIC has more linear dependencies than a WH orbit starting with an arbitrary vector from ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}}: the SIC exhibits 24,935,160 sets of eight linearly dependent vectors while a WH orbit using a vector in ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}} exhibits 24,756,984 (it is this latter value that is shown in Table 2) [31]. This may be connected to the fact that the SIC has a larger automorphism group than an arbitrarily chosen vector. We notice that the Hessian SIC in dimension 3 has more linear dependencies that an arbitrarily chosen vector in the same eigenspace. As SICs can always be found in this smaller subspace when the dimension equals 8 mod 9, one might speculate whether a similar connection to elliptic curves exists in this family of dimensions.

We were unable to collect exhaustive information in dimension 12 regarding linear dependencies, so do not know how many sets of 12 linearly dependent vectors are in a SIC or a WH orbit starting from an arbitrary vector in ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} (or indeed any Zauner subspace). Similarly, we do not know whether their normal vectors exhibit any orthogonality structure analogous to the dimension 6 or 9 cases.

6 Small SICs in dimension N=6N=6

In dimension N=6N=6, among 984 vectors normal to the linear dependent sets generated from an arbitrary fiducial vector in the Zauner subspace (not necessarily a SIC fiducial), we found 30 sets of 4 normal vectors that form 2-dimensional SICs, i.e. in each set, the absolute values for the overlaps between the vectors are 1/31/\sqrt{3} and they lie on a 2-dimensional subspace. This phenomenon also happens in dimension N=9N=9, where 3-dimensional SICs are found among the normal vectors. We refer to SICs of this kind as small SICs (because their dimension is smaller than that of the whole space). Attempts to find such small SICs in dimension N=12N=12 yielded no positive result, perhaps only due to the impracticality of an exhaustive search. In this section, we give an explanation for the small SICs in dimension N=6N=6. In dimension N=9N=9, the phenomenon is not yet fully understood.

The 2-dimensional small SIC sets found in dimension N=6N=6 are all of the form {|ψ⟩,D03|ψ⟩,D30|ψ⟩,D33|ψ⟩}\{\left|{\psi}\right\rangle,D_{03}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle,D_{30}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle,D_{33}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle\}, where Di​jD_{ij}’s are the displacement operators defined in Section 2. As will be proven in the following theorem, for such sets to form a 2-dimensional SIC, |ψ⟩\left|{\psi}\right\rangle just needs to be any normalised eigenvector of U𝒵U_{\mathcal{Z}} that is not in the Zauner subspace. Normal vectors of linearly dependent sets that contain three singlets in the case when the fiducial lies in the Zauner subspace just happen to satisfy this condition, as can been seen from Section 4.

Theorem 4.

In dimension N=6N=6, if |ψ⟩\left|{\psi}\right\rangle is an eigenvector of U𝒵U_{\mathcal{Z}}, then the 4 vectors |ψ⟩,D03|ψ⟩,D30|ψ⟩\left|{\psi}\right\rangle,D_{03}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle,D_{30}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle and D33|ψ⟩D_{33}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle have constant absolute values for their pairwise overlaps. Furthermore, if |ψ⟩\left|{\psi}\right\rangle is not in the Zauner subspace, they span a 2-dimensional subspace and therefore constitute a SIC.

Proof.

If U𝒵|ψ⟩=λ|ψ⟩U_{\mathcal{Z}}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=\lambda\left|{\psi}\right\rangle, then |ψ⟩=λU𝒵†|ψ⟩\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=\lambda U_{\mathcal{Z}}^{\dagger}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle. The first part of the theorem can be proven by noticing that

⟨ψ|D𝐩|ψ⟩=⟨ψ|λ∗U𝒵D𝐩U𝒵†λ|ψ⟩=⟨ψ|D𝒵​𝐩|ψ⟩\left\langle{\psi}\right|D_{\mathbf{p}}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=\left\langle{\psi}\right|\lambda^{*}U_{\mathcal{Z}}D_{\mathbf{p}}U_{\mathcal{Z}}^{\dagger}\lambda\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=\left\langle{\psi}\right|D_{\mathcal{Z}\mathbf{p}}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle (48)

and that the Zauner symplectic matrix 𝒵\mathcal{Z} simply permutes the three points 03, 30 and 33 in phase space according to the following table.

𝐩\mathbf{p} 03 30 33
𝒵​𝐩\mathcal{Z}\mathbf{p} 33 03 30

To prove the second part of the theorem, we need to introduce a square root of the Zauner unitary. Let 𝒲\mathcal{W} be a symplectic matrix given by

𝒲=(1−110)𝒲2=(0−11−1)=𝒵\mathcal{W}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}\hskip 22.76219pt\mathcal{W}^{2}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\ 1&-1\end{pmatrix}=\mathcal{Z} (49)

Let U𝒲U_{\mathcal{W}} be a unitary representative of 𝒲\mathcal{W}, with a phase chosen so that U𝒲2=U𝒵U_{\mathcal{W}}^{2}=U_{\mathcal{Z}}. The eigenspaces of U𝒵U_{\mathcal{Z}} and U𝒲U_{\mathcal{W}} are described in Table 4, where ω=e2​π​i/6\omega=e^{2\pi i/6} and η=e2​π​i/3=ω2\eta=e^{2\pi i/3}=\omega^{2}.

Next we define three new operators R,SR,S and TT as follows.

R=(D03+D30+D33)/3S=(D03+ω2​D30+ω4​D33)/3T=(D03+ω4​D30+ω2​D33)/3\begin{split}R&=(D_{03}+D_{30}+D_{33})/\sqrt{3}\\ S&=(D_{03}+\omega^{2}D_{30}+\omega^{4}D_{33})/\sqrt{3}\\ T&=(D_{03}+\omega^{4}D_{30}+\omega^{2}D_{33})/\sqrt{3}\end{split} (50)

Note that {|ψ⟩,D03|ψ⟩,D30|ψ⟩,D33|ψ⟩}\{\left|{\psi}\right\rangle,D_{03}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle,D_{30}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle,D_{33}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle\} and {|ψ⟩,R|ψ⟩,S|ψ⟩,T|ψ⟩}\{\left|{\psi}\right\rangle,R\left|{\psi}\right\rangle,S\left|{\psi}\right\rangle,T\left|{\psi}\right\rangle\} have the same linear span. We will prove that |ψ⟩∈ℋη\left|{\psi}\right\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{\eta} implies S|ψ⟩=0S\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=0 and R|ψ⟩=|ψ⟩R\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=\left|{\psi}\right\rangle, and that |ψ⟩∈ℋη2\left|{\psi}\right\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}} implies T|ψ⟩=0T\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=0 and R|ψ⟩=−|ψ⟩R\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=-\left|{\psi}\right\rangle. From that one can prove that the span is 2-dimensional.

The following properties of R,SR,S and TT can be derived straightforwardly from their definitions:

S=T†,S2=T2=0,R2=𝟙,S=T^{\dagger},\hskip 14.22636ptS^{2}=T^{2}=0,\hskip 14.22636ptR^{2}=\mathbbm{1}, (51)
S​T=𝟙+R,T​S=𝟙−R.ST=\mathbbm{1}+R,\hskip 39.83385ptTS=\mathbbm{1}-R. (52)

Moreover, S​T/2ST/2 and T​S/2TS/2 are rank-3 projection operators, and they are orthogonal to each other. One can also verify the following commutation relations between R,S,TR,S,T and U𝒲U_{\mathcal{W}}

U𝒲​R=R​U𝒲,U𝒲​S=ω4​S​U𝒲,U𝒲​T=ω2​T​U𝒲.U_{\mathcal{W}}R=RU_{\mathcal{W}},\hskip 14.22636ptU_{\mathcal{W}}S=\omega^{4}SU_{\mathcal{W}},\hskip 14.22636ptU_{\mathcal{W}}T=\omega^{2}TU_{\mathcal{W}}. (53)

These equations tell us how R,SR,S and TT permute the eigenspaces of U𝒲U_{\mathcal{W}}. For example, if |ψ⟩\left|{\psi}\right\rangle is an eigenvector of U𝒲U_{\mathcal{W}} with eigenvalue ω2\omega^{2}, then UWS|ψ⟩=ω4SUW|ψ⟩=S|ψ⟩U_{W}S\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=\omega^{4}SU_{W}\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=S\left|{\psi}\right\rangle, so S|ψ⟩S\left|{\psi}\right\rangle is an eigenvector of U𝒲U_{\mathcal{W}} with eigenvalue 1. The full action of SS and TT on the eigenspaces of U𝒲U_{\mathcal{W}} is described in Figure 2 (RR commutes with U𝒲U_{\mathcal{W}} so it simply leaves the eigenspaces invariant).

Let |k0⟩\left|{k_{0}}\right\rangle, |k1⟩\left|{k_{1}}\right\rangle, |k2⟩\left|{k_{2}}\right\rangle, |k3⟩\left|{k_{3}}\right\rangle and |k4⟩\left|{k_{4}}\right\rangle be non-zero eigenvectors of UWU_{W} belonging to the eigenspaces 𝒦1\mathcal{K}_{1}, 𝒦ω\mathcal{K}_{\omega}, 𝒦ω2\mathcal{K}_{\omega^{2}}, 𝒦ω3\mathcal{K}_{\omega^{3}} and 𝒦ω4\mathcal{K}_{\omega^{4}} respectively. Except for |k0⟩\left|{k_{0}}\right\rangle, the rest of them are unique up to a scalar, because the corresponding eigenspaces are 1-dimensional. As seen from the diagram, we have S|k1⟩=0S\left|{k_{1}}\right\rangle=0. We are going to prove that S|k4⟩=0S\left|{k_{4}}\right\rangle=0, so that S|ψ⟩=0S\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=0 for any |ψ⟩∈ℋη\left|{\psi}\right\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{\eta}.

Suppose otherwise, that S|k4⟩≠0S\left|{k_{4}}\right\rangle\neq 0. It has to be the case that S|k0⟩=0S\left|{k_{0}}\right\rangle=0 (for any choice of |k0⟩\left|{k_{0}}\right\rangle), because otherwise S|k0⟩S\left|{k_{0}}\right\rangle will be a non-zero vector in 𝒦ω4\mathcal{K}_{\omega^{4}}, which is 1-dimensional, which implies S|k0⟩=α|k4⟩S\left|{k_{0}}\right\rangle=\alpha\left|{k_{4}}\right\rangle for some non-zero α\alpha, and therefore S|k4⟩=α−1S2|k0⟩=0S\left|{k_{4}}\right\rangle=\alpha^{-1}S^{2}\left|{k_{0}}\right\rangle=0, contradicting the assumption that S|k4⟩≠0S\left|{k_{4}}\right\rangle\neq 0. Since S|k4⟩S\left|{k_{4}}\right\rangle is a non-zero vector in 𝒦ω2\mathcal{K}_{\omega^{2}}, which is 1-dimensional, we must also have S|k4⟩=β|k2⟩S\left|{k_{4}}\right\rangle=\beta\left|{k_{2}}\right\rangle for some non-zero β\beta, and therefore S|k2⟩=β−1S2|k4⟩=0.S\left|{k_{2}}\right\rangle=\beta^{-1}S^{2}\left|{k_{4}}\right\rangle=0. So from the assumption that S|k4⟩≠0S\left|{k_{4}}\right\rangle\neq 0, we have obtained 0=S|k1⟩=S|k2⟩=S|k0⟩0=S\left|{k_{1}}\right\rangle=S\left|{k_{2}}\right\rangle=S\left|{k_{0}}\right\rangle, which implies 0=TS|k1⟩=TS|k2⟩=TS|k0⟩0=TS\left|{k_{1}}\right\rangle=TS\left|{k_{2}}\right\rangle=TS\left|{k_{0}}\right\rangle, which means that T​STS is orthogonal to the 4-dimensional subspace spanned by 𝒦1\mathcal{K}_{1}, 𝒦ω\mathcal{K}_{\omega} and 𝒦ω2\mathcal{K}_{\omega^{2}}. This contradicts T​S/2TS/2 being a rank-3 projection operator.

Thus, we conclude that S|k4⟩=0S\left|{k_{4}}\right\rangle=0, and that S|ψ⟩=0S\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=0 for any |ψ⟩∈ℋη\left|{\psi}\right\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{\eta}. The identity R|ψ⟩=|ψ⟩R\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=\left|{\psi}\right\rangle immediately follows from 0=TS|ψ⟩=(𝟙−R)|ψ⟩0=TS\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=(\mathbbm{1}-R)\left|{\psi}\right\rangle. Note that T|ψ⟩≠0T\left|{\psi}\right\rangle\neq 0 (because T​STS is orthogonal to S​TST) is a non-zero vector in ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}. T|ψ⟩T\left|{\psi}\right\rangle is not proportional to |ψ⟩\left|{\psi}\right\rangle because T|ψ⟩T\left|{\psi}\right\rangle lies in ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} and |ψ⟩\left|{\psi}\right\rangle lies in ℋη\mathcal{H}_{\eta}. Therefore |ψ⟩\left|{\psi}\right\rangle, R|ψ⟩R\left|{\psi}\right\rangle, S|ψ⟩S\left|{\psi}\right\rangle and T|ψ⟩T\left|{\psi}\right\rangle indeed fully span a 2-dimensional subspace. It’s a similar argument to show that T|k2⟩=0T\left|{k_{2}}\right\rangle=0, which implies T|ψ⟩=0T\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=0 and R|ψ⟩=−|ψ⟩R\left|{\psi}\right\rangle=-\left|{\psi}\right\rangle for any |ψ⟩∈ℋη2\left|{\psi}\right\rangle\in\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}}. ∎

We can thus explain the occurrence of the 22-dimensional SICs one finds when N=6N=6. Unfortunately, one can’t explain the 33-dimensional SICs one finds when N=9N=9 in the same way. If one uses the construction described in the proof of Theorem 4 when N=9N=9 one obtains 9 vectors which do not belong to a 33-dimensional subspace and for which the overlaps are not constant (they actually take two different values). The construction also fails to produce SICs in dimensions 1212 and 1515. We summarise the situation in Table 5, which shows the dimensionality of the subspace spanned by the N2N^{2} vectors obtained using the construction of Theorem 4 as a function of the eigenspace from which |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle is chosen.

Nevertheless, the fact remains that if, in dimension 99, instead of arbitrarily choosing a vector in ℋη\mathcal{H}_{\eta} or ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}} as in Theorem 4, one starts from an arbitrarily chosen fiducial vector |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle in the Zauner subspace (not necessarily a SIC fiducial), then one always does find 33-dimensional SICs among the normal vectors to the linearly dependent sets generated by |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle. If this phenomenon repeated in higher dimensions it would open up the intriguing possibility that one might be able to get a proof of SIC existence in this way.

7 Generalisation to other symplectic unitaries

We have been focussing so far on the Zauner unitary because, along with its conjugates, it is the symplectic unitary which appears to be relevant to the SIC existence problem. However, there are many other symplectic unitaries which give rise to linear dependencies, as we now show.

Before proceeding further we need to take account of a subtlety which is important in even dimensions. Suppose NN is even, so that N¯=2​N\bar{N}=2N. Given 𝒢∈SL⁡(2,ℤN¯)\mathcal{G}\in\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{\bar{N}}) let 𝒢r∈SL⁡(2,ℤN)\mathcal{G}_{r}\in\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{N}) be 𝒢\mathcal{G} reduced mod NN. We define

  1. 1.

    The N¯\bar{N}-order of 𝒢\mathcal{G} to be its order considered as an element of SL⁡(2,ℤN¯)\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{\bar{N}}).

  2. 2.

    The NN-order of 𝒢\mathcal{G} to be the order of 𝒢r\mathcal{G}_{r} considered as an element of SL⁡(2,ℤN)\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{N}).

This distinction was not important in the case of the Zauner matrix since its N¯\bar{N}-order is the same as its NN-order. However, the two orders are, in general, different. Turning to ℤN¯2\mathbb{Z}_{\bar{N}}^{2}, we say that 𝐩\mathbf{p}, 𝐩′∈ℤN¯2\mathbf{p}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\bar{N}}^{2} are NN-distinct if 𝐩′≠𝐩\mathbf{p}^{\prime}\neq\mathbf{p} mod NN. So as to be able to make statements which apply to both even and odd dimensions we will use the terms “NN-order” and “NN-distinct” in odd dimensions also, defining them in the obvious way.

Let 𝒢∈SL⁡(2,ℤN¯)\mathcal{G}\in\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{\bar{N}}) (NN even or odd). We say that 𝒢\mathcal{G} generates linear dependencies in all eigenspaces if, for each eigenvector |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle of U𝒢U_{\mathcal{G}}, there exist 𝐩1,…,𝐩N\mathbf{p}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{p}_{N} which are NN-distinct and such that the vectors

D𝐩1​|ψ⟩,…,D𝐩N​|ψ⟩D_{\mathbf{p}_{1}}|\psi\rangle,\dots,D_{\mathbf{p}_{N}}|\psi\rangle (54)

are linearly dependent.

Continue to suppose 𝒢∈SL⁡(2,ℤN¯)\mathcal{G}\in\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{\bar{N}}), and let nn be the NN-order of 𝒢\mathcal{G}. We say that 𝐩\mathbf{p} is 𝒢\mathcal{G}-full if the points 𝐩,𝒢​𝐩,…,𝒢n−1​𝐩\mathbf{p},\mathcal{G}\mathbf{p},\dots,\mathcal{G}^{n-1}\mathbf{p} are NN-distinct.

We then have

Theorem 5.

Let 𝒢∈SL⁡(2,ℤN¯)\mathcal{G}\in\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{\bar{N}}) and let nn be the NN-order of 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Suppose

  1. 1.

    n>1n>1.

  2. 2.

    NN is a multiple of nn.

  3. 3.

    Tr⁡(U𝒢)≠0\Tr(U_{\mathcal{G}})\neq 0.

  4. 4.

    There exist NN points in ℤN2\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{2} which are NN-distinct and 𝒢\mathcal{G}-full

Then 𝒢\mathcal{G} generates linear dependencies (in the sense defined above) in all eigenspaces.

Proof.

We first observe that U𝒢U_{\mathcal{G}} has at least one eigenspace with dimension <N/n<N/n. In fact, let

U𝒢=ei​θ​∑k=0n−1σk​PkU_{\mathcal{G}}=e^{i\theta}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\sigma^{k}P_{k} (55)

be the spectral decomposition of U𝒢U_{\mathcal{G}}, where σ=e2​π​in\sigma=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{n}} and ei​θe^{i\theta} is a phase. By assumption

0≠Tr⁡(U𝒢)=ei​θ​∑k=0n−1σk​Tr⁡(Pk)0\neq\Tr(U_{\mathcal{G}})=e^{i\theta}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\sigma^{k}\Tr(P_{k}) (56)

It follows that the numbers Tr⁡(Pk)\Tr(P_{k}) cannot all be the same. Consequently we must have Tr⁡(Pk)<N/n\Tr(P_{k})<N/n for at least one value of kk.

It follows from condition 4 that it is possible to choose 𝒢\mathcal{G}-full points 𝐩1,…,𝐩N/n\mathbf{p}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{p}_{N/n} such that the NN points

𝒢r​𝐩j,j=1,…,N/n,r=0,…,n−1\mathcal{G}^{r}\mathbf{p}_{j},\qquad j=1,\dots,N/n,\ r=0,\dots,n-1 (57)

are NN-distinct. Let |ψ⟩|\psi\rangle be any eigenstate of U𝒢U_{\mathcal{G}} and define

|ψj​k⟩=∑r=0n−1σ−r​kD𝒢r​𝐩j|ψ⟩,j=1,…,N/n,k=0,…,n−1|\psi_{jk}\rangle=\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\sigma^{-rk}D_{\mathcal{G}^{r}\mathbf{p}_{j}}|\psi\rangle,\qquad j=1,\dots,N/n,\ k=0,\dots,n-1 (58)

For all kk

|ψj,k⟩∈ℰk,j=1,…,N/n|\psi_{j,k}\rangle\in\mathcal{E}_{k},\qquad j=1,\dots,N/n (59)

where ℰ1,…,ℰn\mathcal{E}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{E}_{n} are the eigenspaces UFU_{F} with the appropriate ordering (note that ℰk\mathcal{E}_{k} isn’t necessarily the eigenspace corresponding to the projector PkP_{k} defined above). We showed that

dimℰk<N/n\dim\mathcal{E}_{k}<N/n (60)

for some kk. For that value of kk the vectors |ψ1,k⟩,…,|ψN/n,k⟩|\psi_{1,k}\rangle,\dots,|\psi_{N/n,k}\rangle are linearly dependent, implying that the vectors

D𝒢r​𝐩j​|ψ⟩,j=1,…,N/n,r=0,…,n−1D_{\mathcal{G}^{r}\mathbf{p}_{j}}|\psi\rangle,\qquad j=1,\dots,N/n,\ r=0,\dots,n-1 (61)

are linearly dependent. ∎

As an illustration of this theorem consider the parity matrix

𝒫=(−100−1)\mathcal{P}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\ 0&-1\end{pmatrix} (62)

We have n=2n=2 and Tr⁡(U𝒫)=2​ei​θ\Tr(U_{\mathcal{P}})=2e^{i\theta} (respectively ei​θe^{i\theta}) if NN is even (respectively odd). Also the number of 𝒢\mathcal{G}-full points in ℤN2\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{2} is N2−4N^{2}-4 (respectively N2−1N^{2}-1) if NN is even (respectively odd). So the theorem shows that 𝒫\mathcal{P} generates linear dependencies in every eigenspace for all even dimensions.

It will be seen that the conditions of the theorem are not very restrictive. There are N2N^{2} points in ℤN2\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{2} so one would expect that the requirement that NN of them be 𝒢\mathcal{G}-full should not be difficult to satisfy. Similarly with the requirement that Tr⁡(U𝒢)≠0\Tr(U_{\mathcal{G}})\neq 0. For a large class of dimensions we can make this statement sharp:

Theorem 6.

Let N=q1​…​quN=q_{1}\dots q_{u} for uu distinct odd prime numbers q1,…,quq_{1},\dots,q_{u}. Then, with the sole exception of the identity matrix, every matrix ∈SL⁡(2,ℤN¯)=SL⁡(2,ℤN)\in\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{\bar{N}})=\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{N}) whose order is a factor of NN generates linear dependencies (in the sense defined above) in every eigenspace.

The proof of this theorem will occupy us for the rest of this section. It depends on the tensor product representation of the Clifford group which is described in Appendix B in [13], and which we now briefly review. For each x∈ℤNx\in\mathbb{Z}_{N} and jj in the range 1,…,u1,\dots,u let xjx_{j} be the unique element of ℤqj\mathbb{Z}_{q_{j}} such that xj=xx_{j}=x mod qjq_{j}. Then the Chinese Remainder Theorem [32] tells us that the map

x↦(x1,…,xu)x\mapsto(x_{1},\dots,x_{u}) (63)

is an isomorphism of the ring ℤN\mathbb{Z}_{N} onto the ring ℤq1×⋯×ℤqu\mathbb{Z}_{q_{1}}\times\dots\times\mathbb{Z}_{q_{u}} with inverse

(x1,…,xu)↦N​κ1​x1q1+⋯+N​κu​xuqu(x_{1},\dots,x_{u})\mapsto\frac{N\kappa_{1}x_{1}}{q_{1}}+\dots+\frac{N\kappa_{u}x_{u}}{q_{u}} (64)

where κj\kappa_{j} is the multiplicative inverse of N/qjN/q_{j} considered as an element of ℤqj\mathbb{Z}_{q_{j}}. Given

𝐩\displaystyle\mathbf{p} =(p1p2)∈ℤN2\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}p_{1}\\ p_{2}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{2} 𝒢\displaystyle\mathcal{G} =(αβγδ)∈SL⁡(2,ℤN)\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\ \gamma&\delta\end{pmatrix}\in\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{N}) (65)
define
𝐩j\displaystyle\mathbf{p}_{j} =(p1​jκj​p2​j)∈ℤqj2\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}p_{1j}\\ \kappa_{j}p_{2j}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{Z}_{q_{j}}^{2} 𝒢j\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{j} =(αjκj−1​βjκj​γjδj)∈SL⁡(2,ℤqj)\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha^{\vphantom{-1}}_{j}&\kappa_{j}^{-1}\beta^{\vphantom{-1}}_{j}\\ \kappa^{\vphantom{-1}}_{j}\gamma^{\vphantom{-1}}_{j}&\delta^{\vphantom{-1}}_{j}\end{pmatrix}\in\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{q_{j}}) (66)

Then define

ϕ\displaystyle\phi :ℤN2→ℤq12⊗⋯⊗ℤqu2\displaystyle\colon\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{2}\to\mathbb{Z}_{q_{1}}^{2}\otimes\dots\otimes\mathbb{Z}_{q_{u}}^{2} ϕ⁡(𝐩)\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{p}) =𝐩1⊗⋯⊗𝐩u\displaystyle=\mathbf{p}_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes\mathbf{p}_{u} (67)
ψ\displaystyle\psi :SL⁡(2,ℤN)→SL⁡(2,ℤq1)⊗⋯⊗SL⁡(2,ℤqu)\displaystyle\colon\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{N})\to\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{q_{1}})\otimes\dots\otimes\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{q_{u}}) ψ⁡(𝒢)\displaystyle\psi(\mathcal{G}) =𝒢1⊗⋯⊗𝒢u\displaystyle=\mathcal{G}_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes\mathcal{G}_{u} (68)

The map ϕ\phi (respectively ψ\psi) is an isomorphism of modules (respectively groups). We have

ϕ⁡(𝒢​𝐩)=ψ⁡(𝒢)​ϕ​(𝐩)\phi(\mathcal{G}\mathbf{p})=\psi(\mathcal{G})\phi(\mathbf{p}) (69)

for all 𝒢\mathcal{G}, 𝐩\mathbf{p}. Let ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n} be nn-dimensional Hilbert space and let

V:ℋN→ℋq1⊗⋯⊗ℋquV\colon\mathcal{H}_{N}\to\mathcal{H}_{q_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes\mathcal{H}_{q_{u}} (70)

be the unitary defined by

V​|x⟩N=|x1⟩q1⊗⋯⊗|xu⟩quV|x\rangle_{N}=|x_{1}\rangle_{q_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes|x_{u}\rangle_{q_{u}} (71)

where |0⟩n,…,|n−1⟩n|0\rangle_{n},\dots,|n-1\rangle_{n} is the standard basis in dimension nn. Then

V​D𝐩​V†\displaystyle VD_{\mathbf{p}}V^{\dagger} =D𝐩1⊗⋯⊗D𝐩u\displaystyle=D_{\mathbf{p}_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes D_{\mathbf{p}_{u}} (72)
V​U𝒢​V†\displaystyle VU_{\mathcal{G}}V^{\dagger} =U𝒢1⊗⋯⊗U𝒢u\displaystyle=U_{\mathcal{G}_{1}}\otimes\dots\otimes U_{\mathcal{G}_{u}} (73)

modulo the phase ambiguity in the definitions of U𝒢,U𝒢1,…,U𝒢uU_{\mathcal{G}},U_{\mathcal{G}_{1}},\dots,U_{\mathcal{G}_{u}}.

Lemma 7.

Let N=q1​…​quN=q_{1}\dots q_{u} for uu distinct odd prime numbers q1,…,quq_{1},\dots,q_{u}. Let 𝒢∈SL⁡(2,ℤN)\mathcal{G}\in\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{N}) be arbitrary. Then the number of 𝒢\mathcal{G}-full points in ℤN2\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{2} is ≥N⁡(q1−1)​…​(qu−1)\geq N(q_{1}-1)\dots(q_{u}-1).

Proof.

Let KK be the number of 𝒢\mathcal{G}-full points in ℤN2\mathbb{Z}^{2}_{N} and KjK_{j} the number of 𝒢j\mathcal{G}_{j}-full points in ℤqj2\mathbb{Z}_{q_{j}}^{2}. Use the isomorphisms defined in Equations (67) and (68) to identify 𝒢\mathcal{G} with 𝒢1⊗⋯⊗𝒢u\mathcal{G}_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes\mathcal{G}_{u} and 𝐩\mathbf{p} with 𝐩1⊗⋯⊗𝐩u\mathbf{p}_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes\mathbf{p}_{u}. Let nn be the order of 𝒢\mathcal{G} and njn_{j} the order of 𝒢j\mathcal{G}_{j}. Then

n=LCM⁡(n1,…,nu)n=\LCM(n_{1},\dots,n_{u}) (74)

Suppose 𝐩j\mathbf{p}_{j} is 𝒢j\mathcal{G}_{j}-full in ℤqj2\mathbb{Z}_{q_{j}}^{2} for each jj. Then

𝒢r​𝐩=𝐩\mathcal{G}^{r}\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{p} (75)

implies rr is a multiple of njn_{j} for each jj, which in turn implies rr is a multiple of nn. So 𝐩\mathbf{p} is 𝒢\mathcal{G}-full in ℤqj2\mathbb{Z}^{2}_{q_{j}}. So K≥K1​…​KuK\geq K_{1}\dots K_{u}. The problem thus reduces to showing that Kj≥qj​(qj−1)K_{j}\geq q_{j}(q_{j}-1) for all jj.

To see this we use the analysis in [33]. Let tj=Tr⁡(𝒢j)t_{j}=\Tr(\mathcal{G}_{j}) and let QjQ_{j} (respectively NjN_{j}) be the set of quadratic residues (respectively non-residues) in ℤqj\mathbb{Z}_{q_{j}}. If tj2−4∈Qjt_{j}^{2}-4\in Q_{j} then 𝒢j\mathcal{G}_{j} is conjugate to a diagonal matrix

𝒢~j=(α00α−1)\tilde{\mathcal{G}}_{j}=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&0\\ 0&\alpha^{-1}\end{pmatrix} (76)

If 𝐩j\mathbf{p}_{j} is non-zero then

𝒢~jr​𝐩𝐣=𝐩𝐣\tilde{\mathcal{G}}_{j}^{r}\mathbf{p_{j}}=\mathbf{p_{j}} (77)

if and only if rr is a multiple of njn_{j}. So Kj=qj2−1K_{j}=q_{j}^{2}-1. If tj2−4∈Njt_{j}^{2}-4\in N_{j} we can diagonalize 𝒢j\mathcal{G}_{j} over the extension field 𝔽qj2\mathbb{F}_{q^{2}_{j}}. So we again have that 𝒢j\mathcal{G}_{j} is conjugate to a matrix of the form

𝒢~j=(α00α−1)\tilde{\mathcal{G}}_{j}=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&0\\ 0&\alpha^{-1}\end{pmatrix} (78)

where α\alpha now belongs to 𝔽qj2\mathbb{F}_{q^{2}_{j}} instead of ℤqj\mathbb{Z}_{q_{j}}. We again deduce that Kj=qj2−1K_{j}=q_{j}^{2}-1. Finally, if tj=±2t_{j}=\pm 2 we have that 𝒢j\mathcal{G}_{j} is conjugate to the matrix

𝒢~j=(±1β0±1)\tilde{\mathcal{G}}_{j}=\begin{pmatrix}\pm 1&\beta\\ 0&\pm 1\end{pmatrix} (79)

for some β\beta. If β=0\beta=0 then Kj=qj2−1K_{j}=q_{j}^{2}-1; otherwise Kj=qj2−qjK_{j}=q_{j}^{2}-q_{j}. ∎

Lemma 8.

Let N=q1​…​quN=q_{1}\dots q_{u} for uu distinct odd prime numbers q1,…,quq_{1},\dots,q_{u}. Then |Tr⁡(U𝒢)|≥1|\Tr(U_{\mathcal{G}})|\geq 1 for all 𝒢∈SL⁡(2,ℤN)\mathcal{G}\in\SL(2,\mathbb{Z}_{N}).

Proof.

In view of Equation (73) it is enough to show that

|Tr⁡(U𝒢j)|≥1|\Tr(U_{\mathcal{G}_{j}})|\geq 1 (80)

for all jj. To see this let

𝒢j=(αβγδ)\mathcal{G}_{j}=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\ \gamma&\delta\end{pmatrix} (81)

We have [33]

U𝒢j={ei​θqj​∑x,y=0qj−1τjβ−1​(δ​x2−2​x​y+α​y2CLOSE​|x⟩​⟨y|β≠0ei​θ​∑x=0qj−1τjα​γ​x2​|α​x⟩​⟨x|β=0U_{\mathcal{G}_{j}}=\begin{cases}\frac{e^{i\theta}}{\sqrt{q_{j}}}\sum_{x,y=0}^{q_{j}-1}\tau_{j}^{\beta^{-1}(\delta x^{2}-2xy+\alpha y^{2}}|x\rangle\langle y|\qquad&\beta\neq 0\\ e^{i\theta}\sum_{x=0}^{q_{j}-1}\tau_{j}^{\alpha\gamma x^{2}}|\alpha x\rangle\langle x|\qquad&\beta=0\end{cases} (82)

where τj=e2​π​iqj\tau_{j}=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{q_{j}}} and ei​θe^{i\theta} is a phase. So

Tr⁡(U𝒢j)={ei​θqj​∑x=0qj−1ωj2−1​β−1​(t−2)​x2β≠0ei​θβ=0,α≠1ei​θ​∑x=0qj−1ωj2−1​γ​x2β=0,α=1\Tr(U_{\mathcal{G}_{j}})=\begin{cases}\frac{e^{i\theta}}{\sqrt{q_{j}}}\sum_{x=0}^{q_{j}-1}\omega_{j}^{2^{-1}\beta^{-1}(t-2)x^{2}}\qquad&\beta\neq 0\\ e^{i\theta}\qquad&\beta=0,\ \alpha\neq 1\\ e^{i\theta}\sum_{x=0}^{q_{j}-1}\omega_{j}^{2^{-1}\gamma x^{2}}\qquad&\beta=0,\ \alpha=1\end{cases} (83)

It would be interesting to see if one can generalise Theorem 6 to the case of even dimensions, and odd dimensions for which the prime factorization contains primes occurring with multiplicity >1>1.

8 Linear dependencies in the monomial representation

In the motivating three-dimensional example there was an interesting interplay between linear dependencies in WH orbits on the one hand, and preferred orthonormal bases on the other. It is not difficult to find fiducial vectors giving rise to a WH orbit with NN linearly dependent sets of NN vectors each, in such a way that their normal vectors form an orthonormal basis: if the generator ZZ is diagonal, any fiducial vector with a zero entry will give rise to such a linearly dependent set under repeated action with ZZ. Acting with XX on the fiducial will permute its entries, and one ends up with NN linearly dependent sets in the orbit.

The situation is more interesting if the dimension is a square number, N=n2N=n^{2}. For this case it has recently been shown that there exists a choice of basis in which the entire Clifford group is represented by monomial matrices, i.e. by permutation matrices in which the unit entries have been replaced by phase factors [13]. This representation stems from the observation that in square dimensions

[Xn,Zn]=0[X^{n},Z^{n}]=0 (87)

Thus XnX^{n} and ZnZ^{n} can be simultaneously diagonalised, and the resulting basis turns out to have the above property. Denote the basis vectors by |r,s⟩|r,s\rangle, where r,sr,s are integers modulo nn, and let us refer to the basis as the monomial basis. The monomial representation of the Clifford group is given by

X|r,s⟩={|r,s+1⟩if​s+1≠0​mod​nqr|r,0⟩if​s+1=0​mod​nX|r,s\rangle=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}|r,s+1\rangle&\mbox{if}\ s+1\neq 0\ \mbox{mod}\ n\\ \\ q^{r}|r,0\rangle&\mbox{if}\ s+1=0\ \mbox{mod}\ n\end{array}\right. (88)
Z|r,s⟩=ωs|r−1,s⟩\displaystyle Z|r,s\rangle=\omega^{s}|r-1,s\rangle (89)

where q=e2​π​inq=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{n}}.

UG|r,s⟩=ei​θτβ−1​(δ​s′2−2​s​s′+α​s2)|δr−γs+mγδ,−βr+αs+mαβ⟩U_{G}|r,s\rangle=e^{i\theta}\tau^{\beta^{-1}(\delta s^{\prime 2}-2ss^{\prime}+\alpha s^{2})}|\delta r-\gamma s+m\gamma\delta,-\beta r+\alpha s+m\alpha\beta\rangle (90)

where

s′=−β​r+α​s+m​αm={0n​is oddn2n​is evens^{\prime}=-\beta r+\alpha s+m\alpha\hskip 22.76219ptm=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}0&&n\ \mbox{is odd}\\ \frac{n}{2}&&n\ \mbox{is even}\end{array}\right. (91)

Note that Equation (90) assumes β\beta is relatively prime to N¯\bar{N}, otherwise one has to use the decomposition given in Equation (14) of Section 2. Evidently the NN orthogonal rays that make up the basis is in itself an orbit of the full Clifford group. Moreover, one sees by inspection that the vector |0,0⟩|0,0\rangle is left invariant by the full symplectic group whenever NN is odd. In this sense the monomial basis is a distant cousin of the ‘special SIC’ in three dimensions—or perhaps of the MUB in three dimensions.

Now suppose that 3|n3|n, and consider the Zauner matrix

𝒵=(0−11−1){\cal Z}=\left(\begin{array}[]{rr}0&-1\\ 1&-1\end{array}\right)\ (92)

If we scrutinise the explicit expression (90) we find that there are three non-zero diagonal elements in the unitary operator U𝒵U_{\cal Z}. If we adjust the phase ei​θe^{i\theta} according to Zauner’s recipe one of them equals η\eta, and the other two equal 11. It follows that any vector in the ℋ1{\cal H}_{1} eigenspace must have one component equal to 0. Since the WH group contains NN diagonal elements (namely the elements of the subgroup generated by XnX^{n} and ZnZ^{n}) this means that the WH orbit generated from a fiducial vector in ℋ1{\cal H}_{1} contains NN vectors confined to a subspace orthogonal to one of the vectors in the monomial basis. Since the entire WH group is given by monomial matrices the orbit can be divided into NN such linearly dependent sets, spanning NN subspaces each orthogonal to a vector in the monomial basis. In particular this applies to the known SICs in these dimensions.

A similar argument applies if 2|n2|n. We consider the symplectic matrix

ℱ=(01−10){\cal F}=\left(\begin{array}[]{rr}0&1\\ -1&0\end{array}\right) (93)

After adjusting the arbitrary phase so that Uℱ4=𝟏U_{\cal F}^{4}={\bf 1} and so that the largest eigenspace corresponds to the eigenvalue 1, we find that UℱU_{\cal F} has two diagonal non-zero elements, one equal to 1 and the other equal to ωN/4\omega^{N/4}. Following the same logic as above we see that every WH orbit that includes a fiducial invariant under UℱU_{\cal F} must be divided into NN linearly dependent sets of NN vectors orthogonal to one of the vectors in the monomial basis.

Variants of this argument can be used also if the dimension is N=k​n2N=kn^{2}, where kk is any integer. In this case the Hilbert space splits into a direct sum of n2n^{2} copies of a kk-dimensional Hilbert space, and there exists a representation of the Clifford group in which every group element acts within and permutes these subspaces [14]. This representation is kk-nomial, in the sense that it is given by a permutation matrix of size n2n^{2} in which the unit entries have been replaced by matrices of size kk. For instance, one finds in dimension eight that any vector in the smallest eigenspace of the Zauner unitary has two zero entries, and again there will be linear dependencies in a WH orbit arising from a fiducial in this eigenspace. A SIC fiducial does in fact exist in this eigenspace [12].

9 Conclusion

The Hesse configuration singles out ‘special SICs’ in dimension 3 by the higher number of linear dependencies among their vectors. We searched for similar patterns in higher dimensions through exhaustive numerical searches for sets of NN linearly dependent vectors in SICs in dimensions N=4N=4 to 8 and partial searches in dimensions N=9N=9 and 12. In dimension 8, the SICs with fiducials in the smallest subspace of the Zauner unitary, ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}}, also stand out for exhibiting a higher number of linear dependencies than other WH orbits with a fiducial vector from the same subspace. This could extend the dimension 3 connection between elliptic curves and SICs (which gives rise to the Hesse configuration) to dimension 8 and, as SIC fiducials always lie in ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}} for dimensions equal to 8 mod 9, possibly to an infinite family of dimensions.

In the dimensions we looked at, sets of NN SIC vectors are usually linearly independent. We proved that it is always possible to find dependencies in SICs for dimensions divisible by 3 (where the SIC fiducials sit in ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1}) and for dimensions equal to 8 mod 9 (where the SIC fiducials sit in ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}}). However, this dependency structure in dimensions divisible by 3 also occurs for any WH orbit when the fiducial vector is taken from ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} and so is not a property uniquely tied to SICs. We also proved that linear dependencies will arise for WH orbits whose fiducial vector is in ℋ1\mathcal{H}_{1} for dimensions N=3​kN=3k; WH orbits whose fiducial vector is in ℋη\mathcal{H}_{\eta} for dimensions N=3​kN=3k and N=3​k+1N=3k+1; and WH orbits whose fiducial vector is in ℋη2\mathcal{H}_{\eta^{2}} for all dimensions. These theorems do not account for all the linear dependencies; our numerical results often revealed a higher number of linearly dependent sets of vectors than the theorems predict.

Looking in detail at linear dependencies in dimension 6 revealed some surprising structure. Firstly, the normal vectors (i.e. the vectors orthogonal to each 5-dimensional subspace spanned by 6 linearly dependent vectors) collect into orthogonal sets of 4 when the HW orbit is a SIC. When the orbit is not a SIC, these normal vectors lose their orthogonality pattern. Secondly, the normal vectors of dependencies from both SICs and non-SICs form 30 2-dimensional SICs. This repeats in dimension 9, where some of the normal vectors form 3-dimensional SICs. We did not find 4-dimensional SICs from normal vectors in dimension 12, but our search was not exhaustive and we cannot rule out their existence either.

We also proved a number of theorems for linear dependencies using unitaries other than the Zauner unitary. Our results represent the beginning of a theory for when linear dependencies occur in WH orbits. This is of interest in itself. Also, just possibly, they may contain an important clue for the SIC existence problem.
